note: Covers five clinical domains with reported accuracy and named limitations, useful as a scoping reference across a hospital estate.
title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Medicine: Challenges Across Diagnostic Imaging, Clinical Decision Support, Surgery, Pathology, and Drug Discovery
explain_beginner: This review looked at how artificial intelligence is used in five areas of medicine: medical scans, tools that help doctors make decisions, surgery, lab tissue analysis, and drug discovery. The author narrowed thousands of records to 150 relevant studies. The review found AI can spot cancers in scans well and can help predict some health problems, guide surgery, assist tissue diagnosis, and speed drug research. But it also found problems: AI can be hard to explain, may reflect biased data, often lacks trials that track patients over time, and faces regulatory barriers. It matters because these tools could improve care, but only with testing and human oversight.
explain_business: This review suggests AI has real potential across five hospital and research areas: imaging, decision support, surgery, pathology, and drug discovery. The evidence base is 150 studies, with strong imaging results, such as cancer detection reaching an AUC of 0.94. Decision support showed mixed real world outcomes, so promised predictions do not always translate into better care. Other areas showed benefits but also face limits. For executives, the practical message is to treat AI as promising but not ready for unchecked routine use. Decisions should fund pilot projects with clear clinical outcomes, bias checks, prospective validation, regulatory review, and human oversight before wider adoption.
explain_practitioner: This review searched PubMed without language or date limits, using controlled terms and free text for AI plus each clinical area. From 2047 records, 243 duplicates were removed, leaving 1804. Title and abstract screening excluded 1482, and full text review excluded 172 more, mostly for missing clinical validation, methodological focus, preclinical work, or not peer reviewed conference abstracts. The final 150 studies were analyzed qualitatively. The review reports strong imaging performance, including cancer detection with AUC up to 0.94. Decision support showed promise for sepsis and atrial fibrillation but mixed real world outcomes. Surgery, pathology, and drug discovery also showed benefits. Key limits were explainability, bias, prospective trials, and regulation.
